transcript.content: Hello, thank you for coming in. Can you tell me what’s been bothering you or what brings you here today?

Yeah, um… honestly, what finally got me to come in is that people keep telling me I’m not listening. Like, not just once in a while — it’s become this thing. My supervisor will be standing right there talking to me, explaining something, and I’ll be looking at him, nodding even, and then a minute later I realize I only caught maybe half of what he said. Then I have to ask him to repeat it, and I can tell he’s getting irritated, like he thinks I don’t care or I’m ignoring him.

And it happens at home too, with my wife. She’ll be telling me something directly, and I swear I’m trying to listen, but then suddenly I realize I missed part of it and I’m like, “Wait, what did you say?” or “Can you say that again?” It’s embarrassing, and it’s causing problems because people think I’m not paying attention on purpose. That’s really the main reason I’m here.
Can you describe if you often find yourself getting distracted easily, even when you're trying to focus on something important?

I’m not totally sure how to answer that, because I don’t always notice it as “getting distracted,” if that makes sense. Like sometimes I’ll be trying to focus on something important and then later realize I wasn’t really with it the whole time, but in the moment I don’t always clock what pulled me away.

When you say distracted, do you mean like noises and people walking by, or more like my mind just jumping somewhere else? Because I can say I do lose the thread of things, but I’m not always aware of what caused it. It’s more like I come back and realize I missed something.
When you lose track of what someone is saying, does it happen more often when you’re feeling particularly anxious, stressed, or worried about something else?

I mean… I don’t think it’s only when I’m anxious or stressed. That’s part of what’s frustrating about it. Like, sure, if I’m worried about something, I might be worse, but this happens even when it’s just a normal conversation.

My supervisor can be standing right in front of me, telling me how he wants something done, and I’m looking at him, I’m not trying to be rude, I’m not walking away or anything… but then a minute later it’s like I realize I only caught half of what he said. Then I have to ask him to repeat it, and I feel stupid because it looks like I wasn’t listening.

Same thing with my wife. She’ll be talking directly to me, not from another room or anything, and I’ll suddenly realize I missed part of it. So I’ll say, “Wait, can you say that again?” and she gets upset because to her it seems like I don’t care. But it’s not just when I’m worked up about something else. It just… happens.

Does this kind of thing happen when you're trying to read something or work on a task that requires concentration, like focusing on a report or following instructions, or is it mainly during conversations?

I guess the thing I’m most aware of is during conversations, because that’s where people actually call me out on it. Like, that’s what got me here, really. My supervisor will be talking straight to me, explaining something, and I’m standing there looking at him, nodding, trying to follow along, and then right after that I realize I only really caught half of it. Then I’m stuck asking him to repeat himself, and it makes me look like I wasn’t listening or like I don’t care.

Same thing with my wife. She’ll be telling me something directly, and a minute later I’m like, “Wait, what did you say?” And I can see it bothers her, because from her side it probably seems like I just tuned her out. But I don’t mean to. I’m not ignoring them on purpose. It’s just like the words went by and I didn’t hold onto all of it.

So, yeah, mostly I notice it when people are talking to me, because that’s when it causes problems right away.

When you're reading something or working on a task that requires focus, like a report or set of instructions, do you find yourself losing track of what you're doing or missing parts of it, even if no one is talking to you?

I’m not really sure, honestly. I mean, at work I’m not usually sitting there reading reports or long instructions the way someone in an office might, so it’s harder for me to compare. A lot of what I do is hands-on, and if there are instructions they’re usually shown to me or told to me, and that’s where I notice it more because somebody is right there and then I have to ask again.

If I’m reading something on my own, I guess I don’t always pay close attention to whether I missed a part unless it causes a problem. Like if I read a form or something and then realize I have to go back over it, I might just think, “Okay, I didn’t catch that,” but I don’t know if that’s the same thing you mean. It doesn’t stand out to me as much as when my wife or supervisor is talking and I realize I didn’t get all of it.

So… I don’t want to say yes if I’m not sure. I’d say I haven’t really noticed it clearly in reading or tasks the same way. It’s mostly the talking-to-me situations that I can point to.

When you're working on tasks that don’t involve conversations, like following steps in a process or focusing on a specific activity, do you find yourself losing focus or making mistakes because your attention slips, even if no one is talking to you?

Yeah… when you put it that way, yes. On the line, if I’m doing something that has steps to it, especially the quality checks, I’ll sometimes rush through them and miss small stuff I should’ve caught. Like a wrong label, or a fitting that’s a little loose, something like that. It’s not like I don’t know I’m supposed to check it. I do know. I’ve done it plenty of times. But I get going fast, trying to keep up, and I guess my attention just kind of jumps ahead to the next thing before I really finish checking what’s in front of me.

And then it comes back on me because my supervisor will pull me aside and be like, “You missed this again,” and that’s embarrassing, because it’s not some complicated thing. It’s little details, but they matter. And the frustrating part is I’ll tell myself, “Okay, slow down, look at everything,” and then when the line is moving and I’m in that rhythm, I still end up blowing past something.

So, yeah, it’s not only when someone is talking to me. I notice it there more because people react right away, but at work with the actual tasks, it happens too.

Outside of work and conversations with your wife, do you notice these kinds of attention issues in other parts of your life — like when you’re driving, doing chores around the house, or trying to relax and read something for fun?

I don’t know that I’ve really paid attention to it in those situations, to be honest. Like, work and my wife are the places where it gets pointed out to me, so those are the ones I can talk about better.

With driving, I mean… I drive, I get where I’m going, but I don’t sit there thinking, “Was I losing focus?” unless something happens, you know? Same with chores around the house. If I don’t finish something or I go back to it later, I might just think I got busy or forgot where I was at, but I’m not sure I’d call it the same thing.

Reading for fun, I don’t really do a whole lot of that, so I can’t say much there. If I’m looking at something on my phone or reading something short, maybe I’ll skim it, but I haven’t noticed it the way I notice it when someone’s talking to me or when I miss a detail at work. So I guess the honest answer is I’m not sure outside of those areas. I don’t want to make it sound worse or say yes just because you listed those examples.
Looking back, were you often distracted or had trouble focusing when you were in school or growing up?

Yeah, looking back, I think I was like this pretty early on. I didn’t think of it that way at the time, obviously — I just thought I was the kid who was always getting in trouble — but teachers were moving my seat all the time because I couldn’t seem to stay put or stop messing with whatever was around me.

I remember getting told a lot to wait my turn, because I’d call out answers before they finished asking the question, or I’d jump in when another kid was working on something. Not even to be mean, I just… I’d see what they were doing and I’d butt in, like, “No, do it this way,” or I’d grab at the paper or try to help when nobody asked me. And then I’d be in trouble again.

That was before middle school, too. It wasn’t just, like, teenage stuff. In elementary school I was already the kid they’d move up front, or away from certain kids, or by the teacher’s desk. At the time I thought teachers just didn’t like me, but now when I look back, yeah, there was definitely a pattern.
